question: A total of \(28\) handshakes was exchanged at the conclusion of a party. Assuming that each participant was equally polite toward all the others, the number of people present was:
solution:
Use the usual convention that every pair of people exchanges exactly one handshake. Let \(n\) be the number of people. Each person shakes hands with the other \(n-1\) people, so the total number of individual participations in handshakes is \(n(n-1)\).

Every handshake contributes exactly two participations, one for each person involved. Thus every handshake is included, with the same multiplicity of two, and
\[
n(n-1)=2\cdot28=56.
\]
Since \(8\cdot7=56\), we get \(n=8\). The product \(n(n-1)\) strictly increases for integers \(n\ge2\), so no other party size gives this total. There were \(\boxed{8}\) people, choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

edges.reason: Contrasting disjoint alternatives with sequential choices helps choose an operation. An array of shirts and trousers establishes the product principle independently of the addition rule.
The criterion distinguishes combinations from permutations, requiring the ordered-selection concept for that contrast even though unordered selection can be introduced independently.

Dividing ordered counts by internal permutations supplies a standard derivation. Evaluating the supplied factorial quotient or a Pascal recurrence does not require first computing a permutation number.
C(n,k) evaluates an unordered selection count; the combination concept gives the object and its non-order-sensitive meaning.
The application criterion computes unordered counts by categories, containing combination-number evaluation within those categories.
edges.scope: computing unordered selection counts in applications

edges.reason: Uniform contributions are often totaled by multiplication, which helps. Double counting itself only needs two summations of one set, and either summation can be done by direct addition.
